records.name: American Samoa
records.summary:
No criminal exposure: the territory's own legislature decriminalised same-sex conduct in the 1979 code revision (effective 1980), age of consent equal at 16. No local protections of practical substance exist: nothing criminalises a trans visitor, and next to nothing shields one.

Partner travel is the sharpest edge. Marriages performed elsewhere must be recognised under a 2022 federal statute, yet the territory performs none: officials long treated the 2015 federal ruling as 'under review', a judge said in 2016 he would not apply it, and licences remain withheld through 2024-26 — a 2026 review concludes any same-sex applicant must be served, but none has applied, so on-island spousal recognition is untested.

Social climate is conservative and church-centred, reserved behaviour expected; yet it is the homeland of a widely accepted indigenous third-gender presence; trans-presenting travellers more often meet cultural familiarity than the hostility recorded in some neighbouring islands. Net: low state risk, thin institutional cover, reliance on informal tolerance.

sources.summary: UH Manoa libraries research guide on Pacific gender identities (maintained; last updated 2026-07-23). Contains substantive American Samoa content: the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS) was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, explicitly re-anchored to cultural pride - 'we are fa'afafine Samoa'. It defines fa'afafine as born male but embodying both male and female traits, 'a recognized and integral part of traditional Samoan culture', and frames colonial suppression followed by contemporary reclaiming of Pacific gender identities.

Out Traveler 'Ask the Expert' column (Ed Salvato, 2009-07-01) answering a honeymoon question about American Samoa: the two Samoan nations share the fa'amatai chiefly system; ASM's ~57,000 residents across seven islands/atolls; 'Samoan culture tends toward traditionalism, and reserved behavior by people of all orientations is expected', yet 'unlike the homophobia rampant in Fiji, homosexuality is a widely accepted part of Samoan culture', with Western gay men reportedly courted by fa'afafine transgender locals and by officially straight men; local artist Dan Taulapapa McMullin calls the Samoan islands 'the homeland of fa'afafine culture'; ASM hotels skew business-travel (Tradewinds, Pago Pago).

The Independent (2015-07-10): American Samoa was then the only US territory unsure whether the 2015 federal marriage ruling applied — its AG said applicability was 'still being reviewed... I don't know' while Puerto Rico, USVI, Guam and CNMI moved to apply it; no licence applications had been made.

American Samoa's Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended the bill be killed. The bill was introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster, who wanted to preempt the kind of marriage lawsuits then unfolding in US states. At the committee hearing, fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine 'don't believe in marriages with other men', describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech who do not seek same-sex marriage, citing Christian upbringing. For this record: documents that the territory deliberately declined a formal marriage ban pre-Obergefell, and gives contemporaneous local fa'afafine voices on the question.

In January 2016 the American Samoa Senate unanimously confirmed former territory Attorney General Fiti Alexander Sunia as District Court judge, filling the seat left by Judge John Ward II's retirement. At his confirmation hearing Senator Tauolo Manaia Fruean, a retired associate judge of the High Court of American Samoa, asked whether Sunia had read Obergefell; Sunia replied he had not read the US Supreme Court decision and that the district court 'doesn't deal with this ruling', and said he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws are changed. For this record: direct evidence that eighteen months after Obergefell the territory's judiciary was operating on the premise it did not automatically apply, with named actors and dates.

2026 law review article by two attorneys practicing in American Samoa (American Samoa Legal Aid, with Freedom From Religion Foundation) concluding that Obergefell DOES apply in the territory despite local officials' statements, and that American Samoa would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied. It records that to date no same-sex couple has applied for a marriage license in the territory, and lays out the litigation roadmap: the High Court of American Samoa first (defendant the Territorial Registrar), then the US Department of the Interior. For this record: the freshest dated authority on the exact open question (is the 2015 ruling operative in ASM?), and it separates the law from the practical reality (no licenses sought/issued).

Samoa News reported in July 2024 an on-island survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, testing whether American Samoa's same-sex marriage ban would survive a challenge under the 14th Amendment. The survey also probes cultural dimensions bearing on the question (collectivistic vs individualistic orientation; linear vs polychronic time). For this record: as of mid-2024, nine years after Obergefell and more than a year after the Respect for Marriage Act obliged recognition of outside marriages (Dec 13 2022), the local ban is treated on-island as operative and its constitutional durability as an open question.

records.name: Northern Mariana Islands
records.summary:
A US commonwealth in political union: federal document, immigration and screening policy applies (including 2025–26 marker restrictions), while marriage recognition reached Saipan in 2015 by operation of the federal constitution — recognition exists, and nothing criminalises same-sex conduct or gender expression. In 2023 the legislature enacted a hate-crimes statute whose sentencing criteria expressly cover sexual orientation and gender identity — a formal, if recent, protection.

The policy accounting is nonetheless near-bottom: a comprehensive US equality index scores the commonwealth's gender-identity law in negative territory (sexual-orientation law 'low'), citing family-law gaps — no second-parent adoption, no assisted-reproduction recognition, no family-services protection. Visitor reality: no documented legal danger, a fresh hate-crime shield, minimal other institutional support, and high social visibility in small, church-influenced islands.

sources.summary: CNMI Public Law 22-32 (signed Jan 2023): amends the Commonwealth Code to provide criteria for enhanced sentencing of defendants for hate-motivated crimes - the hate-crimes statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity.

MAP Equality Profile: Northern Mariana Islands (data as of 27 Sep 2026): Sexual Orientation Policy Score 3.5/22 (Low), Gender Identity Policy Score -2/25 (Negative), overall 1.5/47 (Low); marriage recognition 1/1 since 2015, no comprehensive state nondiscrimination coverage beyond federal EEOC recourse — the scorecard a visitor faces.
Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror): LGBT rights in the Northern Mariana Islands - same-sex marriage legal since 2015 (Obergefell applies), no criminalisation, limited state-level protections.

Wikipedia overview: same-sex marriage legal since 2015 — first same-sex marriage on Saipan officiated 27 July 2015 (per Marianas Variety citation); adoption since 2015; gender changes legal provided the applicant has undergone the specified medical process; discrimination protections limited to government employees beyond federal law. Backs up the blocked wikiwand mirror with canonical content.

Saipan Tribune: the CNMI's first-ever Gay Pride event was held at the GIG Discotheque in Garapan with about 60 people attending; organiser Sharmaine Casquero called it a success — on-the-ground evidence of visible, peaceful LGBT community life in the territory.

records.name: Cook Islands
records.summary:
A self-governing island state in free association with New Zealand, the Cook Islands criminalised male same-sex acts under a 1969 colonial-era Crimes Act (terms to seven or ten years, consent no defence) until parliament repealed the provisions in April 2023, effective 1 June 2023 — after a decade of stalled bills, NZ-assisted drafting, and sustained advocacy by the local Te Tiare Association, whose spokespeople called the laws 'draconian' colonial relics. Enforcement in living memory was essentially absent; the repeal removed a held-over risk rather than an active prosecution threat.

Pre-contact history reframes the present: 2020 coverage noted a nation 'historically accepting of same-sex relationships' whose anti-LGBT sentiment arrived with colonisation. Post-decriminalisation there is still no marriage equality and no general non-discrimination statute; public life is strongly church-inflected; the islands are some 15,000 people where everyone is known — decriminalised, unequal, and small.

sources.summary: PinkNews (14 Apr 2023): Cook Islands parliament voted on Friday to remove the never-enforced 'indecent acts between males' law — exposure of up to 10 years under the 1969 Crimes Act — through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023; a note in the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBTQ+ people, and the bill also adds protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault. Same-sex marriage remains outlawed under the Marriage Amendment Act 2000.

PinkNews (1 Oct 2020): decriminalisation stalled again — MPs deferred the Crimes Bill report by three months. Traces the full path: colonial-era 1969 sections 154/155 (up to 7 years for sex between men) criminalise; a 2017 select committee recommended removing them and 'indecent acts between men'/sodomy were struck from the draft, but MPs later backtracked and the kick-down-the-road continued; notes colonisation introduced the taboo into a historically accepting society.

PinkNews (3 Aug 2017): draft Crimes Bill, written with New Zealand help, would remove sections 154/155 of the 1969 Crimes Act — up to 7 years for gay sex and 5 years for 'any indecent act with or upon any other male', with consent explicitly not a defence. Population 21,000; the country's only LGBTI community group, Te Tiare Association, welcomed the move (member Valentino Wichman quoted on the law's homophobia).

RNZ Pacific (10 Aug 2017): public submissions opened in parliament on the Cook Islands Crimes Bill intended to replace the widely considered outdated 1969 Crimes Act. The clerk of Parliament, John Tangi, confirmed a submission from the Te Tiare Association representing the country's LGBTI community was already before the select committee; at least three lawyers expected to speak on penalties and sentencing.

records.name: Niue
records.summary:
One of the world's smallest self-governing states, in free association with New Zealand, Niue carries neither criminalisation nor protection on LGBT matters. Colonial-era offences were removed with the age of consent reported equalised by 2011, and no audited source documents enforcement against queer people at all; equally there is no recognition of same-sex relationships and no non-discrimination statute — and the principal 1966 act still shows uneven ages of majority by sex (21 men/19 women) on its face into the 2010s.

Culturally, UN regional documentation lists Niue's fakafifine among the Pacific's pre-colonial third-gender identities — 'cultural treasure' framing that signals deep family embedding, coexisting with church-led conservatism. Legacy public-health law provided for HIV testing of visitors staying beyond about two months: rarely invoked, but on the books. With a population near 1,500, anonymity is impossible — the question is community reaction, not arrest, and it is quietly unresolved.

sources.summary: Human Dignity Trust history of criminalisation, Niue section: the Niue Assembly passed the Niue (Sexual Offences) Amendment Act in May (in force June), removing 'buggery', 'attempted buggery' and 'indecent assault on males' — offences under ss.43-44 of the Criminal Law Code carrying up to 10 years. The law was inherited from New Zealand via 1901 annexation, retained on self-governance in 1974, and survived New Zealand's own 1986 decriminalisation (which changed NZ law only). For this record: documented legal decriminalisation and its colonial-law chain.

UN Free & Equal Pacific information sheet (Aug 2015): FAQ on sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status in the Pacific - documents the fakafifine of Niue among the diverse pre-colonial Pacific gender identities that are 'important parts of the cultural treasure of the region'.

GayLawNet Niue laws page: age of majority is 21 for men and 19 for women under the Niue Act 1966 (Part 21, Marriage of Minors); the age of consent was reportedly equalised in May 2011 (per ILGA State-Sponsored Homophobia, May 2011); the page flags limited information available on Niue topics. For this record: dated consent-equality and the sex-asymmetric age of majority still on the books.

records.name: Hong Kong
records.summary:
A special administrative region running its own legal system under a constitutional settlement: trans claims here have been fought in court more than legislated. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and the apex court in 2023 ruled full sex-reassignment surgery must not be a precondition for changing the gender marker on the compulsory identity card — reversing a 2019 high-court loss in the same litigation. Beyond the card, however, recognition still runs on surgery; and where the executive has chosen, it has chosen against: in September 2025 the legislature voted down the government's own registered-partnerships bill 71–14 after court deadlines, so relationship recognition and any SOGI equality ordinance remain absent.

Corporate visibility invites backlash (a bank's rainbow installations drew a homophobic campaign in 2016), and open activism operates in a space tightened since the 2020 security law. Visitor arithmetic: no criminal law, dense urban anonymity, a functioning marker-change route on cards — inside a system that still demands surgery for most recognition and who

sources.summary: AP (Feb 2023): 'Hong Kong transgender men win appeal over status change' — the Court of Final Appeal rules full sex-reassignment surgery should not be a prerequisite for changing the gender marker on official identity cards, a far-reaching win in the Henry Tse case.

PinkNews (1 Feb 2019): HK High Court ruled against trans men Henry Tse, Q and R — Judge Thomas Au's 59-page judgment made full confirmation surgery the 'only objectively ascertainable criterion', rejecting self-ID as leading to 'uncertainty and arbitrariness'; the men had already changed legal gender in Britain; counsel called the requirement 'out of proportion'. Current status per freshness: legal gender recognition still requires full sex-reassignment surgery; Sept 2025 LegCo voted the government's registered-partnerships bill down 71-14.

HKFP opinion by Nury Vittachi (7 Dec 2016), 'HSBC's rainbow lions: Can we have our homophobia back please?': documents the 2016 backlash to HSBC's rainbow-lion installations — a viral local campaign insisting homophobia is homegrown or foreign-imported, framed satirically. Useful as climate evidence: corporate LGBT visibility provokes organised pushback in Hong Kong.

HK Court of Appeal, Leung TC William Roy v Secretary for Justice (CACV317/2005, Sept 2006): judicial review of Crimes Ordinance provisions setting the age of consent for male-male sex at 21 vs 16 for heterosexual acts — the applicant (21, in same-sex relationships since 16) argued the disparity unjustifiably discriminated; the judgment examines whether facially neutral laws can breach equality. Landmark precedent on equal age of consent in Hong Kong.

records.name: Macau
records.summary:
A small southern Chinese territory with its own civil-law system of Portuguese derivation: nothing criminalises same-sex conduct or gender expression, and almost nothing protects them either. There is no legal gender-recognition pathway — the first organised push (2015) got only a hearing at the identification bureau, with the trans claimant speaking behind a screen; when government legislated on domestic violence in 2016 it knowingly excluded same-sex partners as non-'family', against a 2015 UN Committee-Against-Torture direction that protection be non-discriminatory — an exclusion a local association and an internationally known campaigner publicly accused the administration of choosing, warning it signals SOGI bias is justifiable.

For a visitor: zero legal risk, near-zero legal recourse, and the compression of a very small city where casinos, churches and old resident networks all know their own. The administration treats the subject as a non-issue — which is both the mercy and the void.

sources.summary: Macau Daily Times (Feb 2015): Rainbow of Macau met Identification Bureau officials to discuss changing gender on Macau ID documents - one individual ('Avery', speaking behind a screen) sought the change; the first organised push for gender recognition in Macau.

Macau Daily Times (May 2016): Rainbow of Macau criticised the government for excluding same-sex relationships from domestic-violence legislation because same-sex partners were not considered 'family members'.

Jason Chao / Rainbow of Macau statement (May 2016): the government knowingly enacted a discriminatory domestic-violence law despite the UN Committee against Torture's 2015 concluding observations requiring protection without discrimination; warns the law signals that sexual-orientation discrimination is justifiable.

Wikipedia 'LGBTQ rights in Macau': same-sex activity decriminalised 1996; no recognition of same-sex unions; Basic Law Art. 25 discrimination list omits sexual orientation — SOGI protection only in employment (Law 7/2008 Art. 6/2); the 2012 domestic-violence draft dropped same-sex cohabitants for 'lack of social consensus'; the 2015 gender-marker-change study never produced a law.

Plataforma Media (8 Sep 2023): transgender residents cannot change sex on Macau ID cards — no data-change policy exists — causing border-crossing confusion (a trans man holding a Hong Kong card marked male is still registered female in Macau); activists press the long-promised legislative reform.

Plataforma Media (7 Apr 2026): the Justice Services Direction (DSAJ) says gender-identity legal recognition still needs 'prudent study' of core societal values, civil and family law, and states there are 'no plans to revise the framework' — Macau remains the only area in China without ID gender-marker change or sex-reassignment provisions (both possible in mainland China and Hong Kong), despite a 31 March 2026 appeal by four trans residents.
